newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's economic lifeblood in rebel hands.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's economic lifeblood in rebel hands.

text.p: The rebel takeover of Zaire's copper city of Lubumbashi and the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi have cut President Mobutu Sese Seko off from the mineral wealth that has kept him in power for three decades.
Rebels who took up in October seized the Kasai Province capital of Mbuji-Mayi last week before moving on to Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city and capital of southern Shaba Province.
The two provinces hold much of Zaire's vast reserves of diamonds, copper and cobalt. Zaire's main gold producing areas in central and eastern Zaire are also in rebel hands.

Although mining and mineral processing have declined steadily as a share of Zaire's Gross Domestic Product over the past five years, the sector still accounted for 92 precent of export earnings in 1995, industry figures show.
Most of that has traditionally come from the copper mines of Shaba, the diamond mines in Kasai and the gold mines of North and South Kivu provinces where rebels launched their war.

State-owned Generale des Carrieres et des Mines (Gecamines), which is based in Lubumbashi, is Zaire's biggest company and its fortunes have become closely linked with those of the former Belgian colony.

"The fall of Lubumbashi is the total collapse of Mobutu because if Mobutu is intelligent he will realise that he must resign and has no other choice," rebel official Louis Nyarubasa said in the eastern city of Goma.

Societe Miniere de Bakwanga (MIBA), based in Mbuji-Mayi produces most of the world's small industrial diamonds and has been a huge source of government revenue since the decline of copper and cobalt mining to the southwest.
With mining operators still keen on prospects in Zaire, the rebels have already started moves to ease the way for investors to guarantee income from licences and taxes.
Development at the giant Tenke Fengurume copper/cobalt mine in Shaba was virtually unaffected by the fall of Lubumbashi, Tenke Mining Corp President Ted Webb said on Thursday.

Canada's Tenke Mining signed a deal with Zaire's government last December. The first major foreign investment in Zaire since the 1970s, it is a joint-venture with Gecamines who have a 45 percent holding.

In the diamond trading centre of Kisangani, which fell to rebels on March 15, rebels have slashed the cost of an annual licence for an exporter's buying office to $25,000. Under Mobutu it was $150,000. Exporters will pay a tax of 2.5 percent on their purchases to the rebels' government.
Before the rebels took over, Kisangani had about 60 diamond offices run by Lebanese traders and the main one run by Sediza, the De Beers subsidiary in Zaire.
Industry sources said most Lebanese-run offices were partnerships with members of Mobutu's elite.
Mobutu is reputed to be one of the world's richest men.
Industry sources say the true value of Zaire's diamond business is a mystery because an unknown percentage of gems and industrial stones were smuggled out without any record or tax.

But officially, according to Belgian businessman Charles Thys, the annual trade was worth about $360 million for artisanally dug diamonds and $80 million for the production at the country's only modern mine, MIBA, at Mbuji-Mayi, a far bigger diamond centre than Kisangani.
Production of copper and cobalt from mines controlled by Gecamines has been rising steadily since all-time lows in the early 1990s, according to Gecamines.
A recent Gecamines document put 1996 copper output at 38,900 tonnes with 4,000 tonnes for cobalt and 3,159 tonnes for zinc.
Zaire, which produced 14,518 tonnes of cobalt in 1986, remains the world's biggest producer of the commodity.
Copper production plunged from 476,000 tonnes in 1986 to a low of 31,300 in 1994.
